'Your message came at ten past seven,' Elizabeth said, sliding into the seat across from Samir in the library. 'Can we talk at lunch? That's all it said.'

'Yeah.' Samir rubbed the back of his neck. 'I wrote a much worse one last night after the match. Whole paragraph. It's still in my drafts.'

'You didn't send it?'

'I wanted to. My thumb was right there. But I put the phone under the pillow and went to sleep.'

'Why?'

'Everything I wrote sounded like winning, not fixing. This morning I just wanted to hear your side.'

Elizabeth gave a small laugh. 'I was ready to fight, honestly. I had a whole speech.'

'Then let's hear it.'

'Okay. But I go first.'

'Go.'

qa.q: At what time did the short message arrive?
qa.a: The message came at ten past seven and asked whether they could talk at lunch.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling as his thumb hovered over the angry draft?
qa.a: Samir was angry and tempted to send it, wanting to win the argument.

qa.q: What else could Samir do if waiting a night had not cooled things?
qa.a: Samir could write his side down privately or take a walk before contacting Elizabeth, or ask someone he trusts how to start the talk.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth probably feel when the short message arrived?
qa.a: Elizabeth had been ready to fight, so the short message likely came as a surprise and a relief that softened the mood.

grounding: Shows a teenager drafting an angry message, waiting a night, and sending a calmer note asking to talk.

passage:
I'm Sumit, and in Class 10 I had a big fight with my best friend Darshan. He told everyone in our class about something I'd told him in secret.
That night I typed a long message. I called him a traitor and a lot worse. My thumb was on the send button.
Then I remembered Papa saying, "Never decide anything important while angry." So I saved it as a draft and put the phone under my pillow.
I barely slept. But by morning, I read the draft and felt embarrassed. Half of it wasn't even true. I was just hurt.
I deleted it and wrote something shorter: "What you did really hurt me. Can we talk after school?"
He replied in two minutes. "Sorry. Yes."
We talked by the canteen that afternoon. We're still friends. If I'd sent the first one, I don't think we would be.

qa.q: What did Sumit write in the shorter message?
qa.a: "What you did really hurt me. Can we talk after school?"

qa.q: How did Sumit feel on reading the draft in the morning?
qa.a: Sumit felt embarrassed, seeing that half of it wasn't true and was written out of hurt.

qa.q: What else could Sumit do if the anger doesn't fade by morning?
qa.a: Sumit could talk to a trusted adult or wait a little longer before replying, rather than sending anything while still furious.

qa.q: How might Darshan have felt receiving the calm message?
qa.a: Darshan may have felt guilty but relieved, and more willing to apologise because the message asked to talk instead of attacking.

grounding: It shows a teenager who drafts an angry message after a quarrel but waits a night, then writes a calmer note asking to talk.

Hostel warden's note, Wednesday
Around ten last night I found Dhruv in the common room, typing fast, jaw tight. He had fought with his roommate Deepak over a borrowed charger that came back broken, and there had been shouting.
I asked if he was all right. He showed me the message he was about to send. It was angry, and some of it was cruel.
I didn't tell him what to do. I only asked, "Will this still be what you want to say tomorrow?" He thought, saved it as a draft, and went to bed in the spare room I opened for him.
This morning he came to my office. He had deleted the draft. The new message said: "I was angry about the charger. I said things I shouldn't have. Can we sort it out after dinner?"
He sent it in front of me. Deepak replied within the hour. I will check with both boys this evening.
— Warden, Block C

qa.q: What did Dhruv and Deepak fight over?
qa.a: A borrowed charger that came back broken.

qa.q: How was Dhruv feeling when the warden found him in the common room?
qa.a: He was angry and upset, typing fast with a tight jaw after the shouting.

qa.q: Why was waiting a night a better choice than sending the first message?
qa.a: It let Dhruv's anger settle, so he could write something honest and calm instead of cruel words he might regret.

qa.q: How might Deepak experience the calmer message?
qa.a: Deepak may feel relieved and more willing to make up, since the message admits fault and asks to sort it out.

grounding: It shows a teenager who drafts an angry message after a quarrel but waits a night, and by morning writes a calmer note asking to talk.
